title: Gardens and Botany
description: Ten essays, profiles and stories about seeds, flowers, trees and the people who grow them, from Victorian bouquets to an Arctic seed vault.

lessons.title: The Patience of Seeds
lessons.summary: An essay on how a seed reads water, cold and light before it decides to sprout.
lessons.text:
A seed may be the quietest object in the world. It can lie in a drawer or in cold ground for months, sometimes for years, doing nothing that the eye can discern. Yet inside its coat a tiny plant is waiting, and the decision it must one day make is the most dangerous of its life: when to wake up.

A seed that sprouts too early, in a warm week of winter, may be killed by the next frost. A seed that sprouts too late may find the ground already crowded and shaded by faster rivals. It cannot move, and it cannot try again. The timing of that single moment is pivotal, and over millions of years plants have evolved careful ways of getting it right.

No seed consciously decides anything; it has no brain. But it behaves as if it were working through a checklist, and scientists can now discern its items one by one.

The first item is water. Nothing can happen until a dry seed drinks. When it is soaked, the seed swells, and its coat begins to bulge; in a bean left overnight in a glass of water, you can watch the bulge grow. Yet water alone is not enough.

The second item is cold. Many trees and wild flowers of cool regions produce seeds that need weeks of winter chill before they will sprout. Gardeners imitate winter by keeping such seeds in a humid bag in the refrigerator. The seed seems to count the cold days, though not consciously, and only when enough have passed does it treat warmth as a real spring rather than a false one.

The third item is light, and here the science is elegant. When sunlight passes through a prism, it spreads into a band of colors, from violet to red. Green leaves absorb most of the red light and let through more of the "far-red" light that lies just beyond it. Many small seeds contain a pigment that can tell the two apart. In open ground, the pigment signals that the way is clear; under a canopy of leaves, the seed waits. In effect, the seed carries its own small prism.

Field studies show that a young plant's survival is closely correlated with these signals, since plants in a sunny gap do far better than those in deep shade. A seed's caution is correlated with real danger.

Some desert seeds need a heavy rain to wash chemicals out of their coats; others need the smoke of a fire. Across the myriad species of flowering plants, there are myriad versions of the checklist. But everywhere the seed waits for the same pivotal moment, in the dark and the humid soil, until the world outside says yes.

Questions:
Why is the moment when a seed sprouts so pivotal?
If it sprouts too early or too late, it may die, and it cannot try again.
Does a seed consciously decide when to sprout?
No. It has no brain, but it behaves as if it were working through a checklist.
What happens to a seed when it is soaked in water?
It swells, and its coat begins to bulge.
How do gardeners imitate winter for seeds?
They keep the seeds in a humid bag in the refrigerator.
How can a seed tell whether there are leaves above it?
Its pigment can tell red light from far-red light, and under leaves far-red light is stronger.

lessons.title: Saying It with Flowers
lessons.summary: An essay on the Victorian language of flowers, from shy violets to bridal orange blossom.
lessons.text:
Imagine a young woman in London in 1860 who receives a small bunch of flowers from a young man. Before she smiles or frowns, she takes a little book from her shelf. The flowers are violets, a piece of ivy and a single red rose, and the book tells her what they mean: I am shy, I will be true, I love you. The young man has written her a letter without a single word.

This was the language of flowers, and in Victorian Britain it became a popular passion. The idea came from France and spread quickly to Britain and the United States. Avid readers bought these books by the thousands, and an avid collector might own several, each with painted pictures of roses, lilies and violets beside their meanings.

Part of the reason for its popularity lay in the strict manners of the time. It was an age of political liberalism and reform, yet private life followed rules that now seem very narrow. Decency did not allow a respectable young woman to tell a man directly that she liked him, and obedience to her parents was expected in every serious matter. Flowers offered a polite way around these rules. A meek violet could say what a meek young woman could not. The liberalism of public life had not reached the family drawing room, and flowers filled the silence.

The language reached its fullest expression at weddings. When Queen Victoria married in 1840, she wore a wreath of orange blossom in her hair, and orange blossom soon became the most fashionable bridal flower in the country. On the wedding day, bridal flowers were tied to the end of each pew in the church, and the family in the front pew sat beside the finest of them.

Flowers also had a place at the dance. At a ball, a young woman carried a small bouquet, and a partner who asked her for a waltz might glance at it to see what it said. A waltz lasted only a few minutes, but a bouquet could carry its message through the whole evening, within the bounds of decency.

Sorrow had its flowers too. A wreath on the front door told everyone who passed that a family was in mourning.

There was one small problem: the dictionaries rarely agreed. A yellow rose might mean friendship in one book and jealousy in another, so the young man had to know which book the young woman owned. Even so, the old meanings still conjure a vanished world, a time when a handful of violets could conjure a whole conversation, and when obedience to good manners turned a garden into an alphabet.

Questions:
What did the young woman do when she received the flowers?
She took a little book from her shelf to learn what they meant.
Why did the language of flowers become so popular?
Decency did not allow a young woman to speak openly to a man, so flowers offered a polite way around the rules.
What did Queen Victoria wear in her hair when she married?
She wore a wreath of orange blossom, which soon became the most fashionable bridal flower.
Where were flowers placed in the church on a wedding day?
They were tied to the end of each pew.
What was the problem with the dictionaries of flowers?
They rarely agreed, so one flower could have two different meanings.

lessons.title: The Vault in the Mountain
lessons.summary: A report on the seed vault in the Arctic and the first time seeds were taken out of it.
lessons.text:
On the island of Spitsbergen, far north of mainland Norway, a narrow concrete entrance sticks out of the snow on the side of a mountain. It is not monumental. A skier crossing the valley below might take it for a small power station. Yet behind its steel doors lies one of the most monumental projects of modern agriculture: the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, a store of the world's crop seeds.

Around the world, there are hundreds of seed banks, collections that preserve the varieties of wheat, rice, beans and other crops that farmers have grown for thousands of years. A variety that seems useless today may carry the genes to resist a new disease or a hotter climate tomorrow. But seed banks can be lost to fires, floods, power failures and wars. For decades, experts had warned that a single safe place for duplicate samples was overdue. When the vault finally opened in 2008, many said it was long overdue.

The site was chosen with care. The vault lies about 120 meters inside the mountain, well above the level the sea could reach even if the ice caps melted. Inside, the seeds are kept at minus 18 degrees Celsius. If the power ever failed, the frozen rock around the rooms would keep them cold for a long time. The design is meant to be resilient, to survive what ordinary buildings cannot.

The rules are as careful as the rock. The agreements stipulate that each institution that sends seeds keeps ownership of them. The boxes arrive sealed, and Norway does not open them. The agreements also stipulate that only the institution that deposited a box may take it out again. The vault exists for safety, not for utilization: the utilization of these varieties by farmers and breeders depends on the living seed banks around the world.

For seven years, nobody took anything out. Then, in 2015, came the first withdrawal. A research center that had kept a famous collection of crops for dry regions near Aleppo, in Syria, could no longer work there because of the war. For its scientists, it was a long ordeal. They had sent duplicates to the vault in earlier years, and now they asked for them back. They planted the seeds in Lebanon and Morocco, grew fresh harvests, and later returned new samples to the mountain. The ordeal of the collection ended quietly, with seeds simply doing what seeds do.

Visitors are often moved by the boxes on the shelves, sent by countries that rarely agree on anything. The vault cannot transcend every conflict, but in this cold space the shared need for food seems to transcend borders. A skier passing in the winter dark sees only a pale light above the door, and inside, the seeds wait, as resilient as their keepers hoped.

Questions:
Why do seed banks need a backup?
Seed banks can be lost to fires, floods, power failures and wars.
Why would the seeds stay cold if the power failed?
The frozen rock around the rooms would keep them cold for a long time.
What do the agreements stipulate?
Each institution keeps ownership of its seeds, and only it may take its boxes out again.
Why was the first withdrawal made in 2015?
A research center near Aleppo could no longer work there because of the war.
How did the ordeal of that collection end?
The scientists grew fresh harvests in Lebanon and Morocco and returned new samples to the vault.

lessons.title: What the Forest Floor Is Saying
lessons.summary: An essay on the fungal networks under forests and on what has really been proven about them.
lessons.text:
Few scientific ideas have traveled as far in recent years as the idea that trees talk to one another. In books and films, forests are described as communities linked by an underground internet, sometimes called the wood wide web. Old "mother trees" are said to feed their young and to send warnings through it. It is a beautiful picture, but how much of it is true?

The foundation is solid. Most plants live in partnership with fungi. Fine threads of fungus wrap around or enter the roots and spread far into the soil, gathering water and nutrients that roots alone could not reach. In return, the plant gives the fungus sugars made from sunlight. This exchange is ancient and well studied, one of the true nuggets of modern biology.

The next step is also supported. A single fungus can connect to the roots of more than one tree, so in some forests different trees really are linked. In famous experiments published in 1997, researchers in Canada gave young trees carbon with a special label and later found small amounts of that label in nearby trees of another species. Something had moved between them.

Beyond this point, the evidence becomes thinner. In 2023, a team of researchers reviewed the studies behind the popular claims and found serious shortcomings. In many studies, the growth of a young tree was found to correlate with its distance from a large one, but growth can correlate with many things, from water to soil to light. One shortcoming appeared again and again: it was hard to show that the network itself, and not some other path through the soil, had carried the carbon. The reviewers found few solid nuggets of evidence that mature trees send food to their own young.

Why did the popular story run so far ahead of the science? Nobody seems to have misled the public knowingly. Careful researchers often add cautions in a footnote, and a footnote rarely survives in a newspaper. The reviewers also noticed that later papers tended to cite the most positive studies, a habit that could exacerbate the problem. Our love of a good story may exacerbate it further.

None of this means that the forest is silent. Fungi do link many trees, and much remains to be discovered. At a scientific meeting, a keynote speaker might fairly begin with this disclaimer: the network is real, but its powers are still being measured. It is a modest disclaimer, but it is honest, and the rest of such a keynote could still be full of wonder.

Perhaps the best lesson is about reading. When a story about nature seems too perfect, it is worth asking which parts were measured and which were imagined. Trees do not knowingly help their families, as far as anyone can prove, but the threads beneath our feet are remarkable enough without the legend.

Questions:
What do the plant and the fungus exchange?
The fungus gathers water and nutrients, and the plant gives it sugars made from sunlight.
What did the experiments in Canada show?
Carbon given to young trees was later found in nearby trees of another species.
What shortcoming did the reviewers find again and again?
It was hard to show that the network itself had carried the carbon.
Why do cautions often disappear from popular articles?
Researchers put them in a footnote, and a footnote rarely survives in a newspaper.
What disclaimer might a keynote speaker begin with?
The network is real, but its powers are still being measured.

lessons.title: A Fortune in a Bulb
lessons.summary: A short history of the tulip, from Ottoman palace gardens to the famous Dutch boom of 1637.
lessons.text:
Today the tulip is so closely linked with the Netherlands that the two names are almost synonymous. Yet the flower is not Dutch at all. Wild tulips grow in the dry mountains of Central Asia, where they bloom briefly in spring and spend the rest of the year as bulbs under the ground.

The first great lovers of the flower were the Ottomans. In the gardens of Istanbul, gardeners bred new forms with long, pointed petals, and the flower became synonymous with beauty and with the court itself. Around 1720, the court held evening festivities in its gardens, and visitors described tortoises carrying candles on their backs as they wandered slowly among the flowers. No festivity of the age was more famous.

By 1600, bulbs had reached the Netherlands, and there they found perfect conditions: sandy soil, a cool climate and a rich merchant class eager to display its wealth. The most admired flowers were "broken" tulips, whose petals showed flames and feathers of color on a white or yellow ground. We now know that these streaks were caused by a virus carried by small insects, a virus that also weakened the bulbs. A broken flower was therefore hard to produce in quantity, and its price rose.

In the winter of 1636 and 1637, trading in bulbs became a craze. Because bulbs stay in the soil until summer, buyers signed contracts in taverns, promising to pay a fixed price when the bulbs could be lifted. A buyer was obligated to pay whatever the market did, and many buyers sold their promises again within days. Prices rose at a staggering speed. A single rare bulb was said to cost as much as a fine house in Amsterdam, a staggering sum for something the size of an onion. In February 1637, buyers suddenly stopped appearing, and prices fell sharply. Many people who were obligated by contract refused to pay.

For centuries the episode was told as a fable about greed: a whole nation driven mad by flowers and then ruined. Modern historians tell a calmer story. The trade involved a fairly small group of merchants and craftsmen, and the wider economy was hardly damaged. Some traders held a grudge for years against partners who would not pay, but the fable of national ruin was largely invented later.

The flower itself survived and prospered. Dutch growers learned to raise bulbs in vast fields, and the profitability of the trade came to depend on volume rather than on rare prizes. Today the Netherlands produces billions of bulbs each year. A modern marketer sells them in colorful packets, and a clever marketer still tells the old story, because a legend can add to the profitability of any product. Nobody, it seems, holds a grudge against the flower.

Questions:
Where do wild tulips grow?
They grow in the dry mountains of Central Asia.
What did visitors describe at the Ottoman festivities?
They described tortoises carrying candles on their backs among the flowers.
What caused the streaks on broken tulips?
They were caused by a virus carried by small insects.
What was a buyer obligated to do?
A buyer was obligated to pay a fixed price when the bulbs could be lifted.
How do modern historians see the old fable?
They say the trade was small, the economy was hardly damaged, and the fable of national ruin was invented later.

lessons.title: The Keeper of the Greenhouse
lessons.summary: A profile of a botanical garden's curator, a former skiing medalist who cares for a very old tree fern.
lessons.text:
At seven in the morning, before the gates open, Ruth Adler walks through the great greenhouse of the city's botanical garden with a notebook in her hand. The air is warm and wet, and the glass above her is still gray with dawn. She stops at every bed. She touches a leaf here, checks the soil there, and writes a line in the notebook. "Plants cannot tell you when something is wrong," she says. "You have to notice before they do."

Adler has been curator of living collections for eleven years. Her path to the job was not a straight one. In her twenties she was a cross-country skier, and a good one: she was a national medalist twice. After an injury ended her racing, she took a part-time job at the garden, watering plants. "I was clueless," she says, laughing. "I didn't know the difference between a fern and a palm." The former medalist went back to school, studied plant science in the evenings, and slowly climbed through every job the garden offered.

Much of her work is tedious, and she is the first to say so. Each of the garden's twelve thousand plants has a record: where it came from, when it arrived, how it has grown. Keeping those records is tedious, but it is what turns a pretty garden into a scientific collection. A plant without a record, she says, is just decoration.

She is patient with inexperienced staff, perhaps because she remembers being inexperienced herself. "Everyone is clueless at first," she says. Volunteers who give a plant too much water receive a gentle lesson, not a lecture. Only one thing makes her irritated: visitors who pick leaves or seeds to take home. When she is irritated, she reminds herself that these visitors simply love the plants.

The pride of her collection is a tree fern, a tall plant with a trunk like a hairy column and a crown of leaves shaped like feathers. According to the garden's records, it arrived from Australia in 1858 aboard a navy frigate, packed in a sealed glass case that protected it from salt air during the long voyage. The captain of the frigate was a friend of the garden's first director. The fern is now more than 160 years old, and it is still producing new leaves.

In the adjoining house, the climate is warmer still. Here Adler keeps her tropical plants, among them a small zebra plant, named for the white stripes that run across its dark green leaves. Children are always drawn to the zebra plant first. In a room adjoining that house, young plants grow under lights before they move into the displays.

At nine, the gates open and the first visitors arrive. Adler closes her notebook and steps aside. "My favorite moment," she says, "is when someone stops in front of the old fern and just looks up."

Questions:
What does Ruth Adler do before the gates open?
She walks through the greenhouse, checks every bed, and writes notes in her notebook.
What did Adler do before she worked with plants?
She was a cross-country skier and a national medalist twice.
Why does she think keeping tedious records matters?
It turns a pretty garden into a scientific collection.
What makes Adler irritated?
Visitors who pick leaves or seeds to take home make her irritated.
How did the tree fern reach the garden?
It arrived from Australia in 1858 aboard a navy frigate, packed in a sealed glass case.

lessons.title: Flowers That Wait for the Dark
lessons.summary: An essay on the moths and bats that visit flowers at night and the flowers that call them.
lessons.text:
When the sun sets in a summer garden, most flowers close for the night. A few do the opposite. The evening primrose opens its pale yellow petals at sunset, sometimes so quickly that you can watch them move. Others open white flowers as the first stars appear. They have chosen a different public: not bees and butterflies, but the creatures of the night.

Night flowers have much in common. Many are white or very pale, because pale colors are easiest to see in the milky light of the moon. Many have a heavy, sweet scent that travels far on the still evening air. On a warm night, their dizzying perfume can make a visitor feel almost dizzy.

The most skilled visitors are hawk moths. A hawk moth does not land on a flower. It holds itself in the air in front of it, its wings beating too fast to see, and pushes a long tongue deep into the flower's tube to reach the sweet liquid at the bottom. This choreography is like a dance practiced for millions of years: the moth's tongue and the flower's tube have grown to fit each other. Charles Darwin once studied an orchid from Madagascar with a tube nearly a foot long and predicted that a moth with an equally long tongue must exist. Such a moth was found more than twenty years after his death. The choreography he imagined was real.

In warmer countries, bats do much of the night work. Bats roaming over the deserts of Mexico visit the flowers of desert plants, and some travel long distances in a single night. Many of these bats find their way by sound, and some send out their calls through the nose. These nasal calls bounce back from objects around them. A tropical vine has a leaf shaped like a small dish that reflects such nasal calls strongly, so that a roaming bat can find its flowers more easily.

There is something calming about the night garden. Visitors who sit quietly among the pale flowers often describe a kind of trance, a calm attention in which every sound and scent grows sharper. This trance is easiest to reach under a clear sky, with the Milky Way overhead.

One famous night flower belongs to a climbing plant called the queen of the night. Its flower opens for a single night, and gardeners gather to watch it. Within a few hours it grows into a large white star, glows briefly like a small supernova, and is closed by morning. Like a supernova, it is brief and brilliant.

Night flowers face a modern danger. Studies have found that street lights reduce the number of insects visiting flowers at night. The simplest way to help is to turn off the outdoor lights and let the garden keep its night.

Questions:
Why are many night flowers white or pale?
Pale colors are easiest to see in the milky light of the moon.
How does a hawk moth feed from a flower?
It hangs in the air and pushes a long tongue into the flower's tube.
What did Darwin predict?
He predicted that a moth with a very long tongue must exist.
How does the tropical vine help bats find its flowers?
Its leaf is shaped like a small dish and reflects the bats' nasal calls strongly.
What is the simplest way to help night flowers?
Turn off the outdoor lights and let the garden keep its night.

lessons.title: The Cottage Garden
lessons.summary: A gardener in Vermont writes about the old cottage garden tradition and her own crowded plot.
lessons.text:
My garden begins at the back door and ends wherever I run out of space. It is hemmed in by a stone wall on one side and a hedge on the other, and inside that hem of green, almost everything grows together: roses beside cabbages, herbs beside beans, flowers wherever a gap appears. It is a cottage garden, and it belongs to a tradition far older than my small house in Vermont.

The tradition began in the English countryside, among working families who had little land and no money to waste. Their gardens had to feed them. A cottage family grew vegetables, a few fruit trees and herbs for cooking and medicine, and kept chickens and perhaps a pig. Flowers grew in whatever space was left, because they were cheap, pretty and often useful. Nobody planned these gardens to be picturesque.

Later, wealthy writers and painters discovered them. They found the crowded beds picturesque and painted them in soft colors, with tall flowers against white walls. Garden designers began to copy the style on large estates, and the humble cottage garden became a fashion.

Many old cottage plants carry the medicine of the past in their names. One that I love is lungwort, a low plant with spotted leaves and small blue and pink flowers in early spring. People once believed that its spotted leaves looked like diseased lungs, and so they used it to treat pulmonary illness. There is no good evidence that it helped any pulmonary patient, but the old name remains, and so does the plant's quiet charm.

I have added a few touches from this side of the ocean. Along the south side grows a row of blueberry bushes, which give fruit in summer and whose leaves turn bright red in autumn. The blueberry harvest is the high point of my year. Over the gate stands a wooden arbor covered with a climbing rose, and in June the arbor becomes a doorway of flowers.

By the shed sits an old stone trough that once held water for horses. Now it is filled with gravel and tiny mountain plants that need sharp drainage. Stone troughs are a cottage garden favorite.

The garden has its animals too. My hens trot between the beds every afternoon, looking for insects, and the rooster trots behind them as if he were in charge. Each morning the rooster announces the sun to the whole valley. Under the hedge lives a fat brown toad. He eats slugs at night and sits so still by day that visitors take him for a stone. A toad in the garden, the old gardeners said, is worth more than any poison.

A cottage garden is never finished, and that is its pleasure. Each year something spreads, something fails, and something new appears in a gap.

Questions:
What is the writer's garden hemmed in by?
It is hemmed in by a stone wall on one side and a hedge on the other.
Why did the first cottage gardens grow so many different plants?
Working families had to feed themselves from a small piece of land.
Why was lungwort once used to treat pulmonary illness?
People believed its spotted leaves looked like diseased lungs.
What grows over the writer's gate?
A wooden arbor covered with a climbing rose stands over the gate.
What does the toad do in the garden?
He eats slugs at night and sits still like a stone by day.

lessons.title: The Garden on Orchard Street
lessons.summary: Neighbors turn an empty city lot into a garden and save it from being sold after a foreclosure.
lessons.text:
For most of the last century, the lot at the corner of Orchard Street was nobody's favorite place. In 1925 it held an oil derrick, one of hundreds that once stood among the houses of the city. When the well ran dry, the derrick was taken down and a small house was built. The family who lived there later fell behind on their loan, and after the foreclosure the house stood empty until the city tore it down. By 2010, the lot was a square of weeds and broken glass.

Maria Lopez, a retired teacher who lived across the street, decided to change it. She knocked on doors, and twelve families agreed to help. On the first Saturday they filled forty bags with trash. On the second, they built raised beds from old boards. By summer, the lot was full of tomatoes, beans and broccoli, and children were learning that broccoli grows as a thick green head on a tall stalk, not in a plastic bag.

The garden was a grassroots project in the truest sense. Nobody had a grant, and nobody was in charge. When the group needed a water tank, they held a bake sale, and Maria's chocolate brownie became famous on the block. She sold more than three hundred brownie squares in one afternoon.

Then, in 2016, a letter arrived. After the old foreclosure, the lot had passed to the city, and the city was now planning the privatization of dozens of empty lots to raise money. The Orchard Street lot would be sold at auction. A large property conglomerate had already shown interest in buying the whole group of lots.

The gardeners did not panic. They learned the rules of the sale and discovered that a claimant with a strong local interest could ask the city council to delay it. So the garden association became a claimant. Its members gathered more than a thousand signatures and spoke at three council meetings. They argued that privatization should not erase a place that the neighborhood had built with its own hands.

A local land trust offered to help. The conglomerate, which had many other lots to choose from, withdrew its interest, and the land trust became the only claimant. The council agreed to sell the lot to the trust for a small price, on the condition that it remain a garden forever.

On the day of the sale, the mayor came to Orchard Street and read a proclamation naming the third Saturday of June "Orchard Street Garden Day." The proclamation now hangs in a frame on the tool shed. Every year on that day, the gardeners hold a picnic, the grassroots group welcomes new members, and Maria sets out a tray of brownies beside the broccoli.

Questions:
What stood on the lot in 1925?
An oil derrick stood on the lot.
What happened to the house after the foreclosure?
It stood empty until the city tore it down.
How did the gardeners pay for a water tank?
They held a bake sale, and Maria's chocolate brownie became famous on the block.
Why was the lot going to be sold in 2016?
The city was planning the privatization of dozens of empty lots to raise money.
What did the mayor read on the day of the sale?
The mayor read a proclamation naming the third Saturday of June "Orchard Street Garden Day."

lessons.title: A Swamp Noir
lessons.summary: A review of a crime novel about a park ranger who hunts the thieves of a rare orchid in the Florida swamps.
lessons.text:
Most crime novels take place in cities, among wet streets and neon signs. Laura Finch's new novel, "The Ghost in the Swamp," moves the dark mood of noir into the warm, green swamps of southern Florida. It is a noir with mosquitoes instead of cigarette smoke, and it works surprisingly well.

The crime at the center of the book is unusual: the abduction of plants. The victims are ghost orchids, a real and very rare species that grows on the trunks of trees deep in the swamp. A ghost orchid has no ordinary leaves; its white flower seems to float in the air. Collectors will pay thousands of dollars for one, and taking them from the wild is a crime. Finch calls the theft an abduction, and by the end of the book the word no longer seems strange.

The hero is Dana Cole, a park ranger who has worked in the swamp for twenty years. When three orchids vanish in a single week, Dana begins to investigate. Her first lead comes from an informant, an old fishing guide who catches eels for bait and knows every channel in the swamp. The informant tells her that a stranger has been paying local boys to guide him at night. While they talk, the guide pulls an eel from his trap, and the eel twists around his wrist.

The investigation moves step by step. Dana and a sheriff's deputy arrest a young man carrying orchids in a cooler, and they interrogate him for hours. The detainee is frightened and finally names the buyer: a wealthy dealer in rare plants who also sits on the county board. Finch writes the scene in which they interrogate the detainee with restraint; there is no violence, only patience and fear.

The dealer is a clear villain, an abuser of his public office who uses his position to learn where rangers patrol. Finch never lets us doubt his guilt, and that is a strength. Like the best noir, the book is less interested in who did it than in how a quiet place can be harmed by greed.

The showdown takes place on a dark channel at dawn. Dana finds the dealer's boat stuck on a root. He reaches for a revolver, but a large gator suddenly thrashes in the water beside the boat, and the revolver falls into the mud. While the gator thrashes and dives, Dana makes the arrest. It is a strong showdown, though a little convenient.

The book has flaws. Some minor characters are thin, and we learn too little about why this abuser of power became so greedy. But Finch knows the swamp, from the gator in the shallows to the mist on the water, and her love for the real ghost orchid shines through every page.

Questions:
What is the crime at the center of the novel?
The crime is the abduction of ghost orchids from the wild.
Who gives Dana her first lead?
An informant, an old fishing guide who catches eels for bait, gives her the first lead.
What does the detainee finally tell Dana and the deputy?
He names the buyer, a wealthy dealer who also sits on the county board.
What happens during the showdown?
The dealer reaches for a revolver, but a gator thrashes beside the boat and the revolver falls into the mud.
What flaws does the reviewer find in the book?
Some minor characters are thin, and we learn too little about the villain.
